column4: The section stages horses rushing into a gathered force; this verse says no horses or camels were spurred in the acquisition it describes, marking a specific boundary where gain came without the mounted charge.

The section's rider-facing horse and animal service find a direct parallel in this verse's statement that God made livestock for people to ride and eat from, locating the mount within divine provision.

The section contrasts a horse's chest with what is brought out of human chests; this verse says mounts carry people to a need “فِي صُدُورِكُمْ,” joining the rider's bodily transport to the same chest-word in a different, outward-directed sense.
The section ends with what is brought out of the chest and the Lord's full knowledge; this verse says God knows “ذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ” whether speech is hidden or voiced.
The section's human chest is where concealed contents are sifted; this verse says what people hide or disclose within themselves is known to God, a direct parallel to that inward disclosure.

The section turns from the horse's witnessed performance to human accountability; this verse lays out the record and says it omits neither small nor large deeds, making the person's conduct an inspectable account.

The section names horse legs and necks in the Solomon passage, then contrasts the animal with accountable humans; this verse places each person's record around his neck and says it will be brought out open on the resurrection day.

The section's horse races into a crowd before the surah turns to graves; here people emerge from graves rushing as if toward standing stones, reversing the scene into a human rush whose destination is exposed at judgment.

The section makes the horse both a beautiful working body and a coveted possession; this verse calls worldly life adornment and names boasting and competition in wealth, then shows that growth withering away.

After 3:14 names horses among desired possessions, this verse asks about “better than that” and offers gardens and God's approval, giving the list's own stated alternative to attachment to display and wealth.
The section sets the human's love of wealth against remembrance of the Lord; this verse gathers people for Friday prayer and commands them to hasten to God's remembrance and leave trade.
After 62:9 gathers worshippers away from trade, this verse sends them back into the land to seek God's bounty while remembering Him, showing movement and livelihood kept under remembrance.

Following 62:9–10's prayer and return to work, this verse says people disperse toward trade or amusement and leave the Messenger standing; its own contribution is a crowd's movement toward worldly gain over the Lord's message.

Against the section's human whose love of wealth is fierce, this verse describes people whom trade does not distract from God's remembrance, prayer, and almsgiving, while they fear the day hearts and eyes turn about.

After 41:22 names the thought that God did not know their deeds, this verse calls that very assumption ruinous, giving consequence to the hidden conduct and divine knowledge in the section's closing judgment.

The section puts a human on a horse and makes the horse's performance its witness; this verse brings each soul with a driver and a witness. The passage does not say the driver is mounted, so the connection is the role arrangement at judgment rather than a repeated horse scene.

The section opposes the horse's service to its owner with the human's ingratitude to the Lord; this verse places innumerable divine favors beside the human being “ظَلُومٌ كَفَّارٌ,” making ingratitude a response to provision.
